transcript:
Header:
Date: 2026-12-21
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 49 minutes
Attendees: Alex Kim (Redwood AE), Priya Ramesh (Redwood SE), Jordan Lee (AstraWave SRE), Marta Ruiz (Eng Manager), Devon Park (ML Infra)

Summary: quick sync on throughput tuning run, looked at 24h pilot results, agreed on steady-state test and small config tweaks (batch window, concurrency cap).

[00:00] Alex Kim: hey everyone, thanks for carving out time, we'll keep this tight, we have about 50 minutes. main goal is to go over the last 24 hours from the pilot and agree the playbook for next steady-state run.
[01:12] Jordan Lee: yeah, thanks. quick note, we saw a few p99 spikes around 2AM UTC — not sure if that's batch buildup or some… uh, k-v cache warmup?
[02:10] Priya Ramesh: right, so initial look — the KV cache (sometimes transcribed as K-V cash) was cold on a couple of shards after the overnight scale down. you can see the token-generation latency increase when the cache missed. also continuous batching parameters were bumped up at midnight which increased queue depth.
[03:05] Marta Ruiz: when you say bumped up, what exactly changed? we haven't touched the core service.
[03:27] Priya Ramesh: we increased the batch_wait_ms from 25 to 45 to amortize overhead for small requests — that's the platform auto-suggest change for better throughput, but in low-QPS windows it causes head-of-line delays once traffic spikes.
[04:00] Jordan Lee: Hm, that makes sense. So during a sudden burst we see bursts queued and then a big batch that spikes tail latency.
[04:30] Alex Kim: Exactly, and that's where queue shaping helps; we can cap max queue depth and fall back to smaller batch window when queue exceeds threshold. Also we have a concurrency cap per model instance — setting that to a hard cap avoids over-saturating GPU mem and avoids long KV cache thrashing.
[05:12] Devon Park: curious — what's the recommended concurrency target for your quantized 13B model on our dedicated nodes?
[05:38] Priya Ramesh: baseline: for q4_0 we typically see sweet spot at 6-8 concurrent requests per GPU for 16k context median; if you have shorter contexts you can push to 10 but you'll see p95 degrade. Given your mix, I'd recommend starting at 6 and then tune.
[06:10] Marta Ruiz: and burst capacity? can we have extra nodes for traffic spikes?
[06:25] Alex Kim: yes — two options: reserved burst (warm standby with warm KV cache) or on-demand scale where a cold node spins up and will hit cold-cache penalties. Reserved burst costs more but gives consistent tail latency. We mapped cost models in the appendix of the deck — I'll send that.
[07:05] Jordan Lee: got it. the 24h pilot — the median throughput increased by ~18% after enabling continuous batching, but p99 worsened by roughly 40% during spikes.
[07:38] Priya Ramesh: that matches the telemetry. we pulled queue depth histograms and saw the 99th percentile of queue depth jump from 2 to 11 at the spike. That aligns with the batch window change.
[08:15] Alex Kim: action here is to run a steadystate test where continuous batching is enabled but with a dynamic window: batch_wait_ms=25 normally, but if queue_depth>6 then reduce to 15ms and enable immediate flush for small requests.
[09:00] Marta Ruiz: how do you detect queue_depth — is that per-instance or globally?
[09:18] Priya Ramesh: per-instance queue depth. the router annotates request metrics and if instance queue crosses threshold the router will avoid routing new requests to that instance for 2s. It's our soft rotor-shift feature.
[09:58] Jordan Lee: the soft rotor— I've seen router avoid lists, hmm. does that impact fairness?
[10:12] Alex Kim: there's small scheduling jitter but overall improves tail SLOs. We can also rely on concurrency-based admission control which is slightly more predictable.
[10:50] Devon Park: ok, about KV cache warmup — any guidance for pre-warming when adding burst nodes?
[11:05] Priya Ramesh: two paths: proactive prewarm (replay a sample of recent traffic to warm KV entries) or cache seeding from snapshot of hot tokens. Prewarm is easier but needs safe data handling — no PII — it's just token prefixes.
[11:40] Marta Ruiz: we likely want prewarm but need a privacy check. I'll run that by compliance.
[12:05] Jordan Lee: can we see a demo or script for prewarm?
[12:18] Priya Ramesh: yes I'll attach a small script in the ticket. it's our playbook item.
[12:45] Alex Kim: quick pivot — metrics we want for the 12h steady-state run: p50/p95/p99 latency, queue depth histogram, concurrency per instance, tokens/sec, lossless request trace for any flagged errors (500/timeout), and memory/gpu-utilization.
[13:20] Jordan Lee: we'll collect that. question — what cadence should batching adjustments run? like nightly pull?
[13:34] Priya Ramesh: for pilot I'd say single steady-state run with the dynamic window for 12 hours covering your high-peak and trough, then we analyze; afterwards we can consider automated batch tuner which adjusts window every 10 minutes based on recent latency/queue metrics.
[14:10] Marta Ruiz: automated tuner sounds good but we want guardrails — don't want it to oscillate.
[14:25] Alex Kim: agreed; it uses a PID-inspired controller with a 5-minute dampening. we've had success on similar customers.
[15:00] Jordan Lee: any note on model variant fallback? during the morning spike we saw fallback to a smaller quantized shard — was that intended?
[15:22] Priya Ramesh: yes there was a configured fallback path: if instance latency goes beyond 2x target for 60s we reroute new requests to alt model (smaller size) to preserve availability. It trades quality for latency.
[15:50] Devon Park: do we have tooling to measure quality regression when that fallback happens?
[16:05] Priya Ramesh: we can replay a sample prompt set against both variants and compute similarity metrics; Redwood Optimize integrates that into the rollout. We'll include a quality checkset in the deliverables.
[16:40] Alex Kim: important to call out cost impact too — fallback to smaller model lowers per-token cost but may increase error rate; we'll show typical tradeoffs in cost model.
[17:10] Jordan Lee: ok. about autoscaling — we saw a slow scale up in the morning where latency held until new node came up. any ways to speed that?
[17:28] Priya Ramesh: two levers: faster warmup (prewarm) and proactive predict-and-scale where we scale on predicted traffic using recent history. We can also configure minimum replica counts so you never scale to zero overnight.
[18:02] Marta Ruiz: I prefer min replicas for predictability. what's recommended min for our usage?
[18:15] Priya Ramesh: for your baseline QPS, 2 replicas per zone is a safe starting point; with K-V warmup we saw good tail numbers.
[18:45] Alex Kim: let's be pragmatic — include a small reserved burst (1 warm node) in the pilot contract to test economics.
[19:05] Jordan Lee: agreed. can you quantify cost delta?
[19:18] Alex Kim: yes, I'll send numbers — roughly 12-18% uplift depending on region and instance family. We'll include exact line items in the sheet.
[20:00] Devon Park: technical deep dive — we noticed a weird GC bump on one instance around 03:05 that coincided with p99 spike; is that infra or model?
[20:18] Priya Ramesh: likely infra (driver lib) — we saw similar on older kernel versions. we've patched newer infra images; if you want we can run a patched image in pilot.
[20:40] Marta Ruiz: yes please. we also want logs for the GC events.
[20:50] Priya Ramesh: we'll include that in the test artifacts.
[21:22] Alex Kim: quick recap of agreed test plan: 12h steady-state run, continuous batching with dynamic window (25ms normal, 15ms when queue_high), concurrency cap 6, min replicas 2, 1 reserved warm burst node, prewarm script run before test.
[22:05] Jordan Lee: timeline?
[22:12] Alex Kim: Priya runs the test tomorrow (2026-12-23) and uploads traces, Alex sends cost model update by 2026-12-22, AstraWave sends traffic sample by 2026-12-24. Follow-up next week.
[23:00] Marta Ruiz: small ask — can Priya annotate the telemetry with request IDs so we can correlate in our APM?
[23:18] Priya Ramesh: yes we'll add request-id header passthrough and include mapping in the logs.
[24:00] (crosstalk) Speaker 4: uh mm-hmm, sounds good
[25:00] Alex Kim: any other blockers from the customer side?
[25:20] Jordan Lee: compliance sign-off for prewarm is the only blocker, but I think it's straightforward.
[26:00] Devon Park: one more question on queue shaping thresholds — if we set it too low will we see increased errors?
[26:18] Priya Ramesh: if too aggressive we might reject more requests or hit fallback; we'll measure rejected rate and aim <0.2% for production.
[27:00] Marta Ruiz: ok that's acceptable for pilot.
[27:30] Alex Kim: great. I'm going to email the playbook summary after this call.
[28:00] (brief pause)
[28:30] Jordan Lee: also, is the router configurable to avoid certain instances based on GPU temp? we had a thermal event once.
[28:50] Priya Ramesh: yes it's part of health-check routing; we can add thermal metrics to the health probe.
[29:20] Alex Kim: perfect. I'll add that to the test checklist.
[30:00] Jordan Lee: oh — competitor note: ModelServeX does prewarm via snapshot replication but it's more manual; CloudAI Endpoints had autoscale but not batch tuner. Good to know.
[30:30] Alex Kim: good context.
[31:00] Marta Ruiz: any docs we should read before the test?
[31:08] Priya Ramesh: I'll attach the playbook, prewarm script, and the telemetry schema.
[31:45] Jordan Lee: thanks.
[32:00] Alex Kim: closing items: Alex to send cost sheet and contract tweak; Priya to run test and upload traces; Jordan to share workload sample and confirm compliance; schedule follow-up.
[33:10] Devon Park: sounds good. thanks team.
[33:30] Alex Kim: thanks all. end of call.

Post-call notes: attached files to follow: playbook-v1.pdf (link), prewarm_script.sh (link), telemetry-schema.csv (link).
